claim: K2P potassium channels are modulated by volatile anesthetic (VA) drugs.
source: K2P potassium channels are known to be modulated by volatile anesthetic (VA) drugs and play important roles in clinically relevant effects that accompany general anesthesia.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact.

claim: K2P channels play important roles in clinically relevant effects that accompany general anesthesia.
source: K2P potassium channels are known to be modulated by volatile anesthetic (VA) drugs and play important roles in clinically relevant effects that accompany general anesthesia.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact.

claim: A photoaffinity analog of the VA isoflurane was used to identify a VA-binding site in the TREK1 K2P channel.
source: Here, we utilize a photoaffinity analog of the VA isoflurane to identify a VA-binding site in the TREK1 K2P channel.
evidence: This is the primary methodological approach described in the abstract.

claim: The functional importance of the identified VA-binding site was validated by mutagenesis and biochemical modification.
source: The functional importance of the identified site was validated by mutagenesis and biochemical modification.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a validation approach.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations of TREK1 in the presence of VA found multiple neighboring residues on TREK1 TM2, TM3, and TM4 that contribute to anesthetic binding.
source: Molecular dynamics simulations of TREK1 in the presence of VA found multiple neighboring residues on TREK1 TM2, TM3, and TM4 that contribute to anesthetic binding.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from MD simulations.

claim: The identified VA-binding region contains residues that play roles in the mechanisms by which heat, mechanical stretch, and pharmacological modulators alter TREK1 channel activity.
source: The identified VA-binding region contains residues that play roles in the mechanisms by which heat, mechanical stretch, and pharmacological modulators alter TREK1 channel activity and overlaps with positions found to modulate TASK K2P channel VA sensitivity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding about the functional significance of the binding region.

claim: The identified VA-binding region overlaps with positions found to modulate TASK K2P channel VA sensitivity.
source: The identified VA-binding region contains residues that play roles in the mechanisms by which heat, mechanical stretch, and pharmacological modulators alter TREK1 channel activity and overlaps with positions found to modulate TASK K2P channel VA sensitivity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding about the conservation of the binding site.

claim: K2P channels are a group of physiologically important K+ leak channels that modulate cellular resting membrane potential to control excitability.
source: Tandem pore (K2P) potassium channels are a group of physiologically important K+ leak channels that modulate cellular resting membrane potential to control excitability (Enyedi and Czirják, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Human K2P channel abnormalities cause cardiac conduction abnormalities that lead to ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation.
source: Human K2P channel abnormalities cause a wide range of physiological syndromes, including cardiac conduction abnormalities that lead to ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation (Gurney and Manoury, 2009; Friedrich et al., 2014; Decher et al., 2017)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Human K2P channel abnormalities cause familial pulmonary arterial hypertension.
source: Human K2P channel abnormalities cause a wide range of physiological syndromes, including cardiac conduction abnormalities that lead to ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation (Gurney and Manoury, 2009; Friedrich et al., 2014; Decher et al., 2017), familial pulmonary arterial hypertension (Ma et al., 2013)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Human K2P channel abnormalities cause salt-sensitive hyperaldosteronism.
source: Human K2P channel abnormalities cause a wide range of physiological syndromes, including cardiac conduction abnormalities that lead to ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation (Gurney and Manoury, 2009; Friedrich et al., 2014; Decher et al., 2017), familial pulmonary arterial hypertension (Ma et al., 2013), salt-sensitive hyperaldosteronism (Davies et al., 2008)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Human K2P channel abnormalities cause familial migraines.
source: Human K2P channel abnormalities cause a wide range of physiological syndromes, including cardiac conduction abnormalities that lead to ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation (Gurney and Manoury, 2009; Friedrich et al., 2014; Decher et al., 2017), familial pulmonary arterial hypertension (Ma et al., 2013), salt-sensitive hyperaldosteronism (Davies et al., 2008), and familial migraines (Lafrenière et al., 2010; Royal et al., 2019)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: K2P knockout animals exhibit measurable resistance to VA-induced loss of consciousness.
source: K2Ps are proven contributors to the potency of volatile anesthetics (VAs), with K2P knockout animals exhibiting a measurable resistance to VA-induced loss of consciousness (Heurteaux et al., 2004; Pang et al., 2009; Steinberg et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Carotid body TASK channels mediate VA-induced respiratory depression.
source: Systemic effects of VA administration have been directly linked to K2P channel activity, including a role for carotid body TASK channels in mediating VA-induced respiratory depression (Cotten, 2013; Chokshi et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: TREK1 channels mediate the vasodilatory and neuroprotective effects of both polyunsaturated fatty acids and VAs.
source: Systemic effects of VA administration have been directly linked to K2P channel activity, including a role for carotid body TASK channels in mediating VA-induced respiratory depression (Cotten, 2013; Chokshi et al., 2015) and for TREK1 channels in the vasodilatory and neuroprotective effects of both polyunsaturated fatty acids and VAs (Blondeau et al., 2007; Tong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Initial evidence for a VA-induced potassium leak current was found in molluscan pacemaker neurons.
source: Initial evidence for a VA-induced potassium leak current was found in molluscan pacemaker neurons, an activity subsequently determined to be mediated by a member of the TASK K2P subfamily (Franks and Lieb, 1988; Andres-Enguix et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: VA-induced potassium leak current in molluscan pacemaker neurons is mediated by a member of the TASK K2P subfamily.
source: Initial evidence for a VA-induced potassium leak current was found in molluscan pacemaker neurons, an activity subsequently determined to be mediated by a member of the TASK K2P subfamily (Franks and Lieb, 1988; Andres-Enguix et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Studies of snail and human TASK channels identified specific amino acids that alter TASK responsiveness to VAs or eliminate stereoselective discrimination between enantiomeric VA agents.
source: Follow-up studies of both snail and human TASK channels identified specific amino acids that alter TASK responsiveness to VAs or eliminate stereoselective discrimination between enantiomeric VA agents (Andres-Enguix et al., 2007; Conway and Cotten, 2012; Luethy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Findings from TASK channel studies enabled predictions of structural determinants of anesthetic binding within the TASK channel family.
source: These findings enabled predictions of structural determinants of anesthetic binding within the TASK channel family (Bertaccini et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Significant differences in the gating and regulation of divergent K2P subfamilies make it difficult to generalize molecular details of the interactions between VAs and TASK K2P channels to other anesthetic-sensitive K2Ps.
source: However, significant differences in the gating and regulation of divergent K2P subfamilies make it difficult to generalize molecular details of the interactions between VAs and TASK K2P channels to other anesthetic-sensitive K2Ps (Patel et al., 1999), most notably the TREK1 channel.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: TREK1 is a member of a subgroup of K2Ps regulated by membrane stretch or deformation, temperature, and bilayer lipid composition.
source: TREK1 is a member of a subgroup of K2Ps (including TREK1, TREK2, and TRAAK) regulated by the biophysical properties of their surroundings, including membrane stretch or deformation, temperature, and bilayer lipid composition (Honoré, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: In vivo anesthetic potency has long been known to correlate with lipid solubility.
source: VAs are small hydrophobic drugs that readily partition into lipid bilayers and in vivo anesthetic potency has long been known to correlate with lipid solubility, a relationship that holds true over a wide range of structurally diverse anesthetic agents (Sonner and Cantor, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The majority of studies exploring the interaction between anesthetics and ion channels have identified discrete binding sites thought to underlie the modulatory effects of these drugs.
source: While the majority of studies exploring the interaction between anesthetics and ion channels have identified discrete binding sites thought to underlie the modulatory effects of these drugs (Nury et al., 2011; Sauguet et al., 2013; Hemmings et al., 2019)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: A recent study has proposed that in vitro administration of VA agents disrupt membrane lipid rafts, altering phospholipase C activity and modifying the milieu of lipids surrounding TREK1 to modulate its activity.
source: In fact, a recent study has proposed that in vitro administration of VA agents disrupt membrane lipid rafts, altering phospholipase C activity and modifying the milieu of lipids surrounding TREK1 to modulate its activity (Pavel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Azi-isoflurane has been shown to retain the anesthetic effects of isoflurane in animals.
source: Azi-isoflurane has been shown to retain the anesthetic effects of isoflurane in animals, and we first sought to ensure that the chemical modifications present in the azi-isoflurane compound would not alter the effect of this drug on the TREK1 channel.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an established fact.

claim: Application of azi-isoflurane causes a dose-dependent potentiation of mTREK1, with an EC50 of 735 ± 192 µM.
source: Two electrode voltage clamp studies of Xenopus laevis oocytes expressing mouse TREK1 (mTREK1) showed that application of azi-isoflurane causes a dose-dependent potentiation of mTREK1, with an EC50 of 735 ± 192 µM (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding reported in the Results section with reference to Figure 1.

claim: There is no statistically significant difference between the effect of saturating doses of isoflurane or azi-isoflurane on mTREK1 channel function.
source: We found no statistically significant difference between the effect of saturating doses of isoflurane (Patel et al., 1999) or azi-isoflurane on mTREK1 channel function (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding reported in the Results section with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Pairwise alignment of the mouse and zebrafish TREK1 protein primary sequences show 78.3% sequence identity and 89.1% sequence similarity.
source: Pairwise alignment of the mouse and zebrafish TREK1 protein primary sequences show 78.3% sequence identity and 89.1% sequence similarity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct finding from sequence analysis reported in the Results section.

claim: The drTREK1 channel has previously been shown to respond to multiple TREK1 modulatory cues including arachidonic acid and mechanical stretch.
source: The drTREK1 channel has previously been shown to respond to multiple TREK1 modulatory cues including arachidonic acid and mechanical stretch (Brohawn et al., 2014b)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: There is no evidence of differences in the functional behavior of mouse and zebrafish TREK1 orthologues with respect to modulation by azi-isoflurane, temperature, or the TREK1 activator BL1249.
source: we found no evidence of differences in the functional behavior of the two orthologues with respect to modulation by azi-isoflurane, temperature, or the TREK1 activator BL1249 (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), the modulatory cues explored in our study.
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding reported in the Results section with reference to figures.

claim: Mass spectrometry of drTREK1 protein showed evidence of adduction of azi-isoflurane at two residues, G182 and K194, both located on the second transmembrane domain (TM2) of the channel.
source: Following photolabeling, mass spectrometry (MS) of the drTREK1 protein showed evidence of adduction of azi-isoflurane at two residues, G182 and K194, both located on the second transmembrane domain (TM2) of the channel (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding from MS analysis reported in the Results section with reference to Figure 2.

claim: 100-fold excess concentration of isoflurane protected the G182 site from azi-isoflurane photolabeling but did not prevent labeling at K194.
source: The 100-fold excess concentration of isoflurane protected the G182 site from azi-isoflurane photolabeling but did not prevent labeling at K194 (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3), suggesting that only the G182 site is specifically occupied by the parent VA isoflurane.
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding from competitive photolabeling reported in the Results section.

claim: Only the G182 site is specifically occupied by the parent VA isoflurane.
source: The 100-fold excess concentration of isoflurane protected the G182 site from azi-isoflurane photolabeling but did not prevent labeling at K194 (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3), suggesting that only the G182 site is specifically occupied by the parent VA isoflurane.
evidence: This is inferred from the competitive photolabeling experiment.

claim: MS results cover >91% of the drTREK1 protein sequence with high confidence.
source: Although our MS results cover >91% of the drTREK1 protein sequence with high confidence, there are notable regions of the TM3 and TM4 helices that are not identified by MS (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct finding from MS analysis reported in the Results section.

claim: There are notable regions of the TM3 and TM4 helices that are not identified by MS.
source: Although our MS results cover >91% of the drTREK1 protein sequence with high confidence, there are notable regions of the TM3 and TM4 helices that are not identified by MS (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct finding from MS analysis reported in the Results section.

claim: MS on non-photolabeled drTREK1 protein showed essentially the same lack of high confidence coverage within the TM3 and TM4 region.
source: To exclude this possibility, we performed MS on non-photolabeled drTREK1 protein, finding essentially the same lack of high confidence coverage within the TM3 and TM4 region (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding from MS analysis reported in the Results section.

claim: The poor MS coverage of drTREK1 TM3 and TM4 is not the result of photolabeling within these regions.
source: This suggests that the poor MS coverage of drTREK1 TM3 and TM4 is not the result of photolabeling within these regions.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of photolabeled and non-photolabeled samples.

claim: Tryptophan mutagenesis at position 194 had no significant effect on the functional properties of the resultant mutant mTREK1 channels.
source: Tryptophan mutagenesis at position 194 (as well as other more conservative modifications) had no significant effect on the functional properties of the resultant mutant mTREK1 channels (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding from functional assays reported in the Results section.

claim: The amino acid at position 194 is poorly conserved across species.
source: The amino acid at position 194 is poorly conserved across species, a lysine in the drTREK1 gene used for azi-isoflurane photolabeling but an aspartic acid in the mTREK1 construct used for our functional studies.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on sequence comparison.

claim: The D194K mutation had no effect on mTREK1 basal current or temperature dependence.
source: To account for this difference, we introduced a D194K mutant into the mTREK1 background and found that this mutation also had no effect on mTREK1 basal current or temperature dependence (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding from functional assays reported in the Results section.

claim: Position 194 is unlikely to be relevant to the mechanism by which isoflurane and other clinically relevant VAs modulate TREK1.
source: The absence of any observable functional effect of mutation at mTREK1 194, along with the inability of excess isoflurane to protect position 194 from photolabeling by azi-isoflurane, suggest that despite being modified by azi-isoflurane, this site is unlikely to be relevant to the mechanism by which isoflurane and other clinically relevant VAs modulate TREK1.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of functional and photolabeling data.

claim: Position 194 is located at the far end of TM2, facing toward the bulk solution and away from the core of the TREK1 protein.
source: This notion is supported by the location of position 194 at the far end of TM2, facing toward the bulk solution and away from the core of the TREK1 protein.
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis.

claim: TREK1 G182 is located within the center of TM2, one helical turn away from a glycine at position 178 previously shown to be a hinge point for a buckling motion of the TM2 helix that occurs during K2P gating.
source: TREK1 G182 is located within the center of TM2, one helical turn away from a glycine at position 178 previously shown to be a hinge point for a buckling motion of the TM2 helix that occurs during K2P gating (Lolicato et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to support the structural claim.

claim: Tryptophan mutagenesis at mTREK1 G182 demonstrated a large increase in basal current density and a near complete loss of modulation by heat, isoflurane, and the TREK1 activator BL1249.
source: Tryptophan mutagenesis at mTREK1 G182 demonstrated a large increase in basal current density and a near complete loss of modulation by heat, isoflurane, and the TREK1 activator BL1249, findings suggestive of mTREK1 channel activation (Figure 3A–D, note that in Figure 3 panels B-D the concentration of injected cRNA was adjusted to normalize basal current density between mutant and WT mTREK1 channels).
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding from functional assays reported in the Results section.

claim: The effect of mutagenesis at G182 was correlated with the size of the introduced amino acid.
source: By introducing more conservative mutations at G182, we discovered that the effect of mutagenesis was correlated with the size of the introduced amino acid.
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding from functional assays reported in the Results section.

claim: mTREK1 G182A showed only a small potentiating effect on current density and no significant effect on gating by heat.
source: mTREK1 G182A showed only a small potentiating effect on current density and no significant effect on gating by heat and mTREK1 G182C showed an intermediate phenotype (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding from functional assays reported in the Results section.

claim: mTREK1 G182C showed an intermediate phenotype.
source: mTREK1 G182A showed only a small potentiating effect on current density and no significant effect on gating by heat and mTREK1 G182C showed an intermediate phenotype (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding from functional assays reported in the Results section.

claim: MMTS treatment of wild-type mTREK1 channels caused an increase in channel activity that washed out within 2–3 min of removal of MMTS.
source: In wild-type mTREK1 channels, MMTS treatment caused an increase in channel activity that washed out within 2–3 min of removal of MMTS, a seemingly non-specific effect that occurred even in an mTREK1 construct with all five endogenous cysteines removed (mTREK1 cys-).
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding from MMTS modification experiments reported in the Results section.

claim: Modification of the mTREK1 G182C mutant with MMTS caused potentiation of channel activity that persisted after washout of the MMTS reagent.
source: By contrast, modification of the mTREK1 G182C mutant with MMTS caused potentiation of channel activity that persisted after washout of the MMTS reagent (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding from MMTS modification experiments reported in the Results section.

claim: An equivalent effect was observed in an mTREK1 cys- G182C mutant, specifically confirming that it is modification of the G182 cysteine that leads to the observed persistent potentiation of mTREK1 currents following MMTS application.
source: An equivalent effect was observed in an mTREK1 cys- G182C mutant, specifically confirming that it is modification of the G182 cysteine that leads to the observed persistent potentiation of mTREK1 currents following MMTS application (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding from MMTS modification experiments reported in the Results section.

claim: Steric crowding is an important determinant of the potentiation observed after perturbation of the G182 residue.
source: These findings support the notion that steric crowding is an important determinant of the potentiation observed after perturbation of the G182 residue, whether by mutagenesis, MTS reagent modification, or by occupancy with a VA agent or photolabel.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of mutagenesis and MMTS modification experiments.

claim: Activation gating in K2P channels is thought to occur via a 'C-type' gating mechanism involving a rearrangement of the extracellular selectivity filter region.
source: While the G182 residue is located at the cytosolic face of the TREK1 channel, activation gating in K2P channels is thought to occur via a 'C-type' gating mechanism involving a rearrangement of the extracellular selectivity filter region (Bagriantsev et al., 2011; Piechotta et al., 2011; Zilberberg et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to support the claim.

claim: Acidification of the extracellular face of TREK1 has been shown to inhibit channel activity and to simultaneously diminish potassium selectivity.
source: Acidification of the extracellular face of TREK1 has been shown to inhibit channel activity and to simultaneously diminish potassium selectivity, a hallmark of selectivity filter-based gating (Cohen et al., 2008; Sandoz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to support the claim.

claim: The mTREK1 G182W channel was resistant to closure by acid.
source: While the mTREK1 WT and mTREK1 D194W mutants were both strongly inhibited by application of extracellular acidosis, the mTREK1 G182W channel was resistant to closure by acid (Figure 3H, IpH5.5/pH9.0 0.15 ± 0.05 for mTREK1 WT, 0.17 ± 0.1 for mTREK1 D194W, 0.51 ± 0.08 for mTREK1 G182W)
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding from pH sensitivity assays reported in the Results section.

claim: The IC50 of the acid effect was similar for mTREK1 WT, D194W, and G182W channels.
source: although the IC50 of the effect was similar for all three channels tested (pH 7.88 ± 0.07 for mTREK1 WT, 7.63 ± 0.08 for mTREK1 D194W, and 7.59 ± 0.07 for mTREK1 G182W).
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding from pH sensitivity assays reported in the Results section.

claim: The mTREK1 G182W channel was resistant to the effects of BL1249.
source: In line with these observations, the mTREK1 G182W channel was also resistant to the effects of BL1249 (Figure 3D and I), a TREK1 activator believed to act by promoting potassium ion occupancy within the selectivity filter (Schewe et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding from BL1249 sensitivity assays reported in the Results section.

claim: BL1249 is a TREK1 activator believed to act by promoting potassium ion occupancy within the selectivity filter.
source: In line with these observations, the mTREK1 G182W channel was also resistant to the effects of BL1249 (Figure 3D and I), a TREK1 activator believed to act by promoting potassium ion occupancy within the selectivity filter (Schewe et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Isoflurane modulation of the TREK1 channel occurs via anesthetic binding to the G182 site causing allosteric stabilization of the selectivity filter 'C-type' gate.
source: These data support a mechanistic model in which isoflurane modulation of the TREK1 channel occurs via anesthetic binding to the G182 site causing allosteric stabilization of the selectivity filter 'C-type' gate, which leads to increased TREK1 channel activity.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on the experimental data.

claim: Many of the biophysical modalities known to modulate TREK1 channels are believed to alter channel activity by affecting the selectivity filter 'C-type' gate.
source: Many of the biophysical modalities known to modulate TREK1 channels, including heat, mechanical stretch, intracellular acidosis, and bioactive lipids, are believed to alter channel activity by affecting the selectivity filter 'C-type' gate (Bagriantsev et al., 2011; Bagriantsev et al., 2012; Piechotta et al., 2011)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to support the claim.

claim: The input sensor for biophysical gating cues is thought to be the intracellular C-terminal domain.
source: though the input sensor for these biophysical gating cues is thought to be the intracellular C-terminal domain (Honoré et al., 2002; Chemin et al., 2005b; Bagriantsev et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to support the claim.

claim: Structurally defined 'TM4 up' and 'TM4 down' conformational states have been identified as the key rearrangements that allow C-terminal domain inputs to traverse the protein and converge at the selectivity filter to modulate gating.
source: Structurally defined 'TM4 up' and 'TM4 down' conformational states Brohawn et al., 2014a; Lolicato et al., 2014; Dong et al., 2015 have been identified as the key rearrangements that allow these C-terminal domain inputs to traverse the protein and converge at the selectivity filter to modulate gating (Zhuo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to support the claim.

claim: VA occupancy at the G182 site could modulate TREK1 activity by influencing TM4 intramolecular rearrangements known to play a key role in K2P gating.
source: Within this gating model, the location of the G182 anesthetic-binding site along the TM2 helix in direct opposition to TM4 (Figure 4C) is intriguing. It suggests that VA occupancy at the G182 site could modulate TREK1 activity by influencing TM4 intramolecular rearrangements known to play a key role in K2P gating.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis proposed based on structural considerations.

claim: A pocket formed by G182 and the nearby TM3 and TM4 helices had the highest ranked score and was the only predicted binding site near the G182 residue in docking analysis.
source: A pocket formed by G182 and the nearby TM3 and TM4 helices had the highest ranked score and was the only predicted binding site near the G182 residue.
evidence: This is a direct finding from computational docking analysis reported in the Results section.

claim: Simulation of WT mTREK1 in the presence of VA demonstrated isoflurane to be highly mobile within the binding pocket.
source: Simulation of WT mTREK1 in the presence of VA demonstrated isoflurane to be highly mobile within the binding pocket, adopting a range of positions (Figure 5B) and ultimately escaping the binding site after approximately 360 ns of simulation during trajectory 1.
evidence: This is a direct finding from MD simulation reported in the Results section.

claim: The observed high degree of isoflurane mobility is consistent with both the low binding affinity predicted by docking analysis and the high concentrations of isoflurane required to activate TREK1 in functional assays.
source: This observed high degree of isoflurane mobility is consistent with both the low binding affinity predicted by docking analysis and the high concentrations of isoflurane required to activate TREK1 in functional assays.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MD simulation results in the context of other data.

claim: The two independent MD trajectories converge on a number of high occupancy positions.
source: The two independent MD trajectories converge on a number of high occupancy positions (Table 1, Figure 5A), with occupancy defined as the percentage of MD trajectory snapshots in which the isoflurane ligand was within 7 Å of a given residue.
evidence: This is a direct finding from MD simulation reported in the Results section.

claim: MD simulations demonstrated that isoflurane remained in close proximity to the G182 residue for >94% of the time VA occupied the binding site.
source: In agreement with our photolabeling findings, MD simulations demonstrated that isoflurane remained in close proximity to the G182 residue for >94% of the time VA occupied the binding site.
evidence: This is a direct finding from MD simulation reported in the Results section.

claim: Isoflurane imposes a consistent steric crowding at the G182 position.
source: This finding supports the notion that isoflurane imposes a consistent steric crowding at the G182 position, akin to the activity enhancing modifications we introduced through either mutagenesis or biochemical modification.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MD simulation results in the context of experimental data.

claim: The isoflurane molecule did not induce any major conformational changes in mTREK1 during either of the simulation trajectories.
source: The isoflurane molecule did not induce any major conformational changes in mTREK1 during either of the simulation trajectories, and we did not observe any alteration in the position of the TM4 helix attributable to the presence of isoflurane.
evidence: This is a direct finding from MD simulation reported in the Results section.

claim: Localized increases in RMSD were found within the VA-binding pocket at mTREK1 F185 and I189 (TREK1 + Isoflurane MD trajectory 1) or F214 (TREK1 + Isoflurane MD trajectory 2).
source: However, we found localized increases in RMSD within the VA-binding pocket at mTREK1 F185 and I189 (TREK1 + Isoflurane MD trajectory 1) or F214 (TREK1 + Isoflurane MD trajectory 2) (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is a direct finding from MD simulation reported in the Results section.

claim: Side-chain rotameric orientation was clearly altered at F185, I189, and F214 positions by the presence of the isoflurane ligand.
source: These localized deviations in RMSD were absent when we limited our analysis to the main chain Cα carbon (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), and we found that side-chain rotameric orientation was clearly altered at these positions by the presence of the isoflurane ligand (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a direct finding from MD simulation reported in the Results section.

claim: The F185 residue has previously been shown to impact K2P responsiveness to heat, VAs, mechanical stretch, and the pharmacological efficacy of BL1249.
source: The F185 residue has previously been shown to impact K2P responsiveness to heat, VAs, mechanical stretch, and the pharmacological efficacy of BL1249, a K2P activator (Lolicato et al., 2014; Dong et al., 2015; Luethy et al., 2017; Pope et al., 2018)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to support the claim.

claim: F185 is known to form a pi-stacking interaction with the TM3 F214 residue.
source: and is known to form a pi-stacking interaction with the TM3 F214 residue (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an established fact.

claim: The F185/Y214 interaction has been proposed to stabilize the 'TM4-down' gating conformation in TREK2 channels.
source: This F185/Y214 interaction has been proposed to stabilize the 'TM4-down' gating conformation in TREK2 channels (Dong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: In the mTREK1 WT and mTREK1 G182W simulations, pi-stacking between F185 and F214 occurred in 37% and 38% of trajectory frames, respectively.
source: In the mTREK1 WT and mTREK1 G182W simulations, pi-stacking between these residues occurred in 37% and 38% of trajectory frames, respectively, but pi-stacking occurred in less than 2% of the trajectory frames in both of the isoflurane-bound wild-type mTREK1 simulations (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a direct finding from MD simulation reported in the Results section.

claim: Pi-stacking between F185 and F214 occurred in less than 2% of the trajectory frames in both of the isoflurane-bound wild-type mTREK1 simulations.
source: In the mTREK1 WT and mTREK1 G182W simulations, pi-stacking between these residues occurred in 37% and 38% of trajectory frames, respectively, but pi-stacking occurred in less than 2% of the trajectory frames in both of the isoflurane-bound wild-type mTREK1 simulations (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a direct finding from MD simulation reported in the Results section.

claim: In TREK1 + isoflurane MD simulation trajectory 1, the isoflurane ligand directly interrupts the pi-stacking interaction between F185 and F214.
source: In TREK1 + isoflurane MD simulation trajectory 1, the isoflurane ligand directly interrupts the pi-stacking interaction (Figure 6B and F)
evidence: This is a direct finding from MD simulation reported in the Results section.

claim: In trajectory two, it is the ligand induced reorientation of the F214 rotamer that is responsible for disrupting the pi-stacking interaction.
source: while in trajectory two it is the ligand induced reorientation of the F214 rotamer that is responsible for disrupting the pi-stacking interaction (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is a direct finding from MD simulation reported in the Results section.

claim: After the isoflurane molecule escapes from its binding site during trajectory 1, the F185/F214 interaction remained disrupted due to the isoflurane induced reorientation of the F185 sidechain.
source: Even after the isoflurane molecule escapes from its binding site during trajectory 1 (Figure 6D), the F185/F214 interaction remained disrupted due to the isoflurane induced reorientation of the F185 sidechain.
evidence: This is a direct finding from MD simulation reported in the Results section.

claim: The structural model that serves as the starting point for MD simulations is in the mTREK1 'TM4-up' state.
source: However, it is also possible that VA binding induces a conformation distinct from either of these two structurally defined states. The molecular mechanisms governing the connectivity between TM4 conformation and the flux gating behavior of the selectivity filter (Schewe et al., 2016) remains poorly defined and is an area of significant ongoing interest.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as context for the MD simulations.

claim: The F185/F214 interaction is predicted to favor the 'TM4-down' conformation of mTREK1.
source: While additional sampling time might have allowed the F185/F214 interaction to eventually re-establish, the structural model that serves as the starting point for our simulations is in the mTREK1 'TM4-up' state and the F185/F214 interaction is predicted to favor the 'TM4-down' conformation of mTREK1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: In the neighboring unliganded subunit of mTREK1, there was no evidence of F185/F214 pi-stacking.
source: In the neighboring unliganded subunit of mTREK1, we found no evidence of F185/F214 pi-stacking, lending support to the idea that pi-stacking between these two residues is generally disfavored in the 'TM4-up' state (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a direct finding from MD simulation reported in the Results section.

claim: A combination of VA-induced local structural perturbations, disruption of the F185/F214 pi-stacking interaction, and direct steric effects upon TM4 movement all combine to alter the dynamics of the TM4 movements known to influence K2P gating.
source: Based on our MD findings, we hypothesize that a combination of VA-induced local structural perturbations, disruption of the F185/F214 pi-stacking interaction, and direct steric effects upon TM4 movement all combine to alter the dynamics of the TM4 movements known to influence K2P gating.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis proposed based on the MD simulation results.

claim: The TRAAK K2P channel is anesthetic insensitive.
source: Although both TREK and TASK channels are potentiated by VA agents, the TRAAK K2P channel is anesthetic insensitive (Patel et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: TRAAK is 44% identical and 69% homologous to TREK1.
source: TRAAK is 44% identical and 69% homologous to TREK1, and the two channels share many functional properties, including modulation by heat, mechanical stretch, pH, and arachidonic acid (Maingret et al., 1999; Kang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a fact about sequence similarity.

claim: TREK1 and TRAAK share many functional properties, including modulation by heat, mechanical stretch, pH, and arachidonic acid.
source: TRAAK is 44% identical and 69% homologous to TREK1, and the two channels share many functional properties, including modulation by heat, mechanical stretch, pH, and arachidonic acid (Maingret et al., 1999; Kang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to support the claim.

claim: There was no evidence of azi-isoflurane photolabeling at the conserved glycine or at any other position in the hTRAAK channel.
source: The G182 residue identified by azi-isoflurane photolabeling of drTREK1 is conserved in the hTRAAK sequence, but we found no evidence of azi-isoflurane photolabeling at this glycine or at any other position in the hTRAAK channel (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct finding from photolabeling experiments reported in the Results section.

claim: MS of hTRAAK protein after photolabeling showed a relatively lower total coverage of the hTRAAK sequence compared to results for drTREK1 (84% for hTRAAK versus 91% for drTREK1).
source: MS of hTRAAK protein after photolabeling showed a relatively lower total coverage of the hTRAAK sequence compared to our results for drTREK1 (84% for hTRAAK versus 91% for drTREK1)
evidence: This is a direct finding from MS analysis reported in the Results section.

claim: All hTRAAK residues homologous to the drTREK1 azi-isoflurane binding region identified by MD simulations were positively identified by MS.
source: but all hTRAAK residues homologous to the drTREK1 azi-isoflurane binding region identified by MD simulations were positively identified, precluding the possibility that azi-isoflurane binds within this region of hTRAAK.
evidence: This is a direct finding from MS analysis reported in the Results section.

claim: The inability of VA agents to activate TRAAK channels is due to either an absence of binding or a significantly reduced affinity of anesthetic for the VA binding region.
source: Our results suggest that the inability of VA agents to activate TRAAK channels is due to either an absence of binding or a significantly reduced affinity of anesthetic for this VA binding region.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the photolabeling and MS results.

claim: Four residues differ significantly between the mTREK1 and mTRAAK sequences at positions that showed the highest isoflurane occupancy during MD simulations.
source: We next explored the sequence similarity between mTREK1 and mTRAAK at the residues that showed the highest isoflurane occupancy during MD simulations. Amongst the identified amino acids, we found four residues that differ significantly between the mTREK1 and mTRAAK sequences (Figure 7A–B)
evidence: This is a direct finding from sequence comparison reported in the Results section.

claim: The 'TRAAK-like' mutant mTREK1 channels all exhibit diminished responsiveness to the potentiating effect of isoflurane.
source: When examined by TEVC, the 'TRAAK-like' mutant mTREK1 channels all exhibit diminished responsiveness to the potentiating effect of isoflurane (Figure 7C), supporting a role for these residues in either forming the VA binding domain or transducing the effects of binding to channel opening.
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding from functional assays reported in the Results section.

claim: The effect of combining two TRAAK-like mutations was additive, as shown for the double mutant mTREK1 F185L G186R.
source: While the extent of the effect of these mutants was less dramatic than the near complete absence of isoflurane responsiveness in the G182W mutant, the effect of combining two TRAAK-like mutations was additive, as shown for the double mutant mTREK1 F185L G186R (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding from functional assays reported in the Results section.

claim: The 'TRAAK-like' mutants maintain their sensitivity to activation by heat.
source: Although the G182W mutant exhibited diminished responsiveness to both VA activation and heat, the 'TRAAK-like' mutants maintain their sensitivity to activation by heat (Figure 7D–E).
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding from functional assays reported in the Results section.

claim: The 'TRAAK-like' mutants selectively alter VA activation without significantly perturbing gating by heat.
source: The fact that the 'TRAAK-like' mutants selectively alter VA activation without significantly perturbing gating by heat argues for their specificity to the mechanism of action of VAs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional assay results.

claim: Activation of TREK1 by heat is known to be critically related to the phosphorylation state of serine 333 in the intracellular C-terminal domain of TREK1.
source: Activation of TREK1 by heat is known to be critically related to the phosphorylation state of serine 333 in the intracellular C-terminal domain of TREK1 (Maingret et al., 2000)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The persistence of mTREK1 heat activation in 'TRAAK-like' mutants suggests that these mutations do not eliminate VA modulation by simply causing a global activation of the mTREK1 'C-type' gate.
source: and the persistence of mTREK1 heat activation in these 'TRAAK-like' mutants suggests that these mutations do not eliminate VA modulation by simply causing a global activation of the mTREK1 'C-type' gate (as was the case for the G182W mutant).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional assay results.

claim: The 'TRAAK-like' mutations appear to reduce VA sensitivity by acting specifically at the VA site of action.
source: Rather, the 'TRAAK-like' mutations appear to reduce VA sensitivity by acting specifically at the VA site of action, consistent with predictions made by our MD simulation data and mTREK1 vs mTRAAK sequence homology.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional assay results in the context of MD simulation and sequence data.

claim: The VA isoflurane binds to a TREK1 TM2 residue in close proximity to the previously proposed VA modulatory site in TASK K2P channels.
source: By utilizing an unbiased photolabeling approach, we show that the VA isoflurane binds to a TREK1 TM2 residue in close proximity to the previously proposed VA modulatory site in TASK K2P channels.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the Discussion section based on the experimental findings.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulation studies show that isoflurane is mobile within the newly identified TREK1-binding site and interacts with residues from TM2, TM3, and TM4.
source: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation studies based on our photolabeling findings show that isoflurane, a known low-affinity ligand for TREK1, is mobile within this newly identified TREK1-binding site and interacts with residues from TM2, TM3, and TM4.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the Discussion section based on the MD simulation findings.

claim: Isoflurane interactions include key molecular contacts with residues known to influence the conformational rearrangement of the TM4 helix that drive K2P modulation by heat, mechanical stretch, and other pharmacological channel modulators.
source: These interactions include key molecular contacts with residues known to influence the conformational rearrangement of the TM4 helix that drive K2P modulation by heat, mechanical stretch, and other pharmacological channel modulators (Dong et al., 2015; Lolicato et al., 2014; Brohawn et al., 2014a; Pope et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a summary statement in the Discussion section based on the MD simulation findings with citations.

claim: Multiple point mutations within the putative VA-binding pocket specifically diminished TREK1 VA responsiveness without otherwise perturbing channel function.
source: Our photolabeling and MD results enabled us to design multiple point mutations within the putative VA-binding pocket that specifically diminished TREK1 VA responsiveness without otherwise perturbing channel function.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the Discussion section based on the mutagenesis findings.

claim: The data support the notion of a shared VA modulatory site across the TREK and TASK K2P subfamilies.
source: Our data support the notion of a shared VA modulatory site across the TREK and TASK K2P subfamilies and suggest a mechanism by which binding of VA within this site promotes conformational rearrangements known to gate K2P channels.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the Discussion section based on the overall findings.

claim: Binding of VA within the identified site promotes conformational rearrangements known to gate K2P channels.
source: Our data support the notion of a shared VA modulatory site across the TREK and TASK K2P subfamilies and suggest a mechanism by which binding of VA within this site promotes conformational rearrangements known to gate K2P channels.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion stated in the Discussion section based on the overall findings.

claim: A single point mutation in the lymneal TASK TM3 residue M159 caused loss of steroselective discrimination between R and S optical isomers of isoflurane.
source: Prior to our study, the strongest evidence for a VA-binding site in K2P channels was found in the TASK subfamily, where a single point mutation in the lymneal TASK TM3 residue M159 (homologous to TREK1 position T211) caused loss of steroselective discrimination between R and S optical isomers of isoflurane (Andres-Enguix et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: TREK1 T211 lies within a span of the TM3 helix that could not be resolved with MS.
source: TREK1 T211 lies within a span of the TM3 helix we were unable to resolve with MS but through MD simulation we identified T211 as a determinant of TREK1 VA binding (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the MS and MD simulation findings.

claim: Through MD simulation, T211 was identified as a determinant of TREK1 VA binding.
source: TREK1 T211 lies within a span of the TM3 helix we were unable to resolve with MS but through MD simulation we identified T211 as a determinant of TREK1 VA binding (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the MD simulation findings.

claim: TREK1 F185 and M291 align to positions implicated in TASK VA sensitivity.
source: Two additional residues identified by MD simulation, TREK1 F185 and M291, also align to positions implicated in TASK VA sensitivity (Andres-Enguix et al., 2007; Conway and Cotten, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: All three residues (F185, T211, M291) differ significantly in the TRAAK protein sequence.
source: All three residues (F185, T211, M291) differ significantly in the TRAAK protein sequence and 'TRAAK-like' mutations at these positions decreased TREK1 VA sensitivity (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on sequence comparison and functional data.

claim: 'TRAAK-like' mutations at F185, T211, and M291 decreased TREK1 VA sensitivity.
source: All three residues (F185, T211, M291) differ significantly in the TRAAK protein sequence and 'TRAAK-like' mutations at these positions decreased TREK1 VA sensitivity (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on functional data.

claim: The overlapping molecular determinants of TREK1 and TASK1 VA sensitivity suggest a shared VA-binding site across the K2P family.
source: The overlapping molecular determinants of TREK1 and TASK1 VA sensitivity (and of TRAAK VA insensitivity) suggest a shared VA-binding site across the K2P family.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section based on the overall findings.

claim: Recent work demonstrates that bupivacaine binding constrains TM4 helix movement and ultimately alters selectivity filter behavior in TASK1 channels.
source: While the gating mechanisms of TASK channels have not been as extensively studied as those of the mechanosensitive K2Ps, recent work exploring the inhibitory effect of the local anesthetic agent bupivacaine on TASK1 channels demonstrates that bupivacaine binding constrains TM4 helix movement and ultimately alters selectivity filter behavior (Rinné et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The bupivacaine site of action in TASK channels differs from the VA modulatory site identified in this study.
source: The bupivacaine site of action in TASK channels differs from the VA modulatory site identified in our study, but the effect of drug binding on TM4 conformation may be a shared feature in K2P gating utilized by both local and general anesthetics.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a comparison with other findings.

claim: The effect of drug binding on TM4 conformation may be a shared feature in K2P gating utilized by both local and general anesthetics.
source: The bupivacaine site of action in TASK channels differs from the VA modulatory site identified in our study, but the effect of drug binding on TM4 conformation may be a shared feature in K2P gating utilized by both local and general anesthetics.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the Discussion section.

claim: VAs modulate K2P channel activity by influencing the position of the TM4 helix.
source: Our data suggest that VAs modulate K2P channel activity by influencing the position of the TM4 helix.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion stated in the Discussion section based on the overall findings.

claim: The MD simulation data do not show major TM4 conformational rearrangements in the presence of isoflurane.
source: However, the MD simulation data do not show major TM4 conformational rearrangements in the presence of isoflurane and thus whether VAs induced TM4 movements.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a limitation of the MD simulation findings.

claim: There is evidence to suggest that both the 'TM4 up' and 'TM4 down' conformations can promote active K2P channel states.
source: As there is evidence to suggest that both the 'TM4 up' and 'TM4 down' conformations can promote active K2P channel states (McClenaghan et al., 2016), each of the two conformations could be consistent with a VA-activated channel.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Both the direct steric constraints imposed by the presence of VA near TM4 and the disruption of the 'TM4 down' state stabilizing F185/F214 pi-stacking interaction would be predicted to favor a 'TM4 up' conformation.
source: However, both the direct steric constraints imposed by the presence of VA near TM4 and the disruption of the 'TM4 down' state stabilizing F185/F214 pi-stacking interaction would be predicted to favor a 'TM4 up' conformation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic prediction stated in the Discussion section based on the findings.

claim: The molecular mechanisms governing the connectivity between TM4 conformation and the flux gating behavior of the selectivity filter remains poorly defined.
source: However, it is also possible that VA binding induces a conformation distinct from either of these two structurally defined states. The molecular mechanisms governing the connectivity between TM4 conformation and the flux gating behavior of the selectivity filter (Schewe et al., 2016) remains poorly defined and is an area of significant ongoing interest.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The obsolete VAs chloroform and diethyl-ether activate TREK1 and TASK3 but paradoxically inhibit the TASK1 channel.
source: For instance, while the obsolete VAs chloroform and diethyl-ether activate TREK1 and TASK3, they paradoxically inhibit the TASK1 channel (Patel et al., 1999; Andres-Enguix et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: Nitrous oxide and xenon have been reported to activate TREK1 but have no effect on TASK channels.
source: Nitrous oxide and xenon have been reported to activate TREK1 but have no effect on TASK channels (Gruss et al., 2004)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: THIK channels are inhibited by the VAs halothane and isoflurane.
source: Meanwhile, little is known about the gating of THIK channels but they are inhibited by the VAs halothane and isoflurane, an effect that appears to play an important role in the clinically relevant central respiratory depressant effect of VA administration (Rajan et al., 2001; Lazarenko et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: The VA-binding site identified in this study represents only one of a subset of VA modulatory domains in the K2P family.
source: One explanation would be that the VA-binding site identified in our study represents only one of a subset of VA modulatory domains in the K2P family.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the Discussion section to explain inconsistent VA responses.

claim: There are numerous examples of VA-responsive ion channels that feature multiple low-affinity anesthetic modulatory sites acting in a combinatorial fashion.
source: Within the anesthetic mechanisms literature there are numerous examples of VA-responsive ion channels that feature multiple low-affinity anesthetic modulatory sites acting in a combinatorial fashion to produce a given output (Fourati et al., 2018; Heusser et al., 2018; Woll et al., 2018; Hemmings et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: VA binding to a single site may produce opposing effects in the context of subtle differences in the connectivity between TM4 movements and the channel gate.
source: However, the location of the identified K2P VA-binding site at a position central to TM4 gating offers an alternative explanation. We understand relatively little about the mechanism by which TM4 movements govern K2P channel activity and it is possible that VA binding to this single site may produce opposing effects in the context of subtle differences in the connectivity between TM4 movements and the channel gate.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the Discussion section to explain inconsistent VA responses.

claim: Recent studies demonstrate that the resting and activated conformation of the TM4 helix in TREK1 versus TRAAK channels are inverted.
source: Recent studies utilizing the state-dependent binding of the mechanosensitive K2P inhibitor fluoxetine demonstrate that the resting and activated conformation of the TM4 helix in TREK1 versus TRAAK channels are inverted, underscoring this point (Soussia et al., 2018) and perhaps contributing to the absence of VA binding and responsiveness in TRAAK channels.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The TREK1 channel is strongly modulated by its surrounding membrane environment.
source: The TREK1 channel is strongly modulated by its surrounding membrane environment, with lipid headgroup as well as acyl-chain length and saturation playing roles in shaping K2P functional behavior (Chemin et al., 2005a; Chemin et al., 2005b; Cabanos et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: In prokaryotic ligand gated ion channels, binding sites for anesthetics and lipids have been found to overlap.
source: In prokaryotic ligand gated ion channels, binding sites for anesthetics and lipids have been found to overlap (Nury et al., 2011; Prevost et al., 2012)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: Numerous structural studies of K2P channels have identified bound lipids, but none of these lipid-binding sites overlap with the VA-binding site identified in this study.
source: While numerous structural studies of K2P channels have identified bound lipids, none of these lipid-binding sites overlap with the VA-binding site identified in our study (Brohawn et al., 2014a; Dong et al., 2015; Lolicato et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: An MD simulation study of TREK2 has shown that a lipid can bind to a site akin to the TREK1 VA-binding site and that this bound lipid restricts the movement of TM4 in response to a simulated membrane stretch.
source: Despite this absence of structural evidence, an MD simulation study of TREK2 has shown that a lipid can bind to a site akin to our TREK1 VA-binding site and that this bound lipid restricts the movement of TM4 in response to a simulated membrane stretch (Aryal et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Numerous residues within the VA-binding site are likely to be determinants of both lipid and VA modulation of K2P channel gating.
source: While we suspect that multiple sites on the TREK1 channel may ultimately play important roles in the modulatory effects of lipids, numerous residues within the VA-binding site are likely to be determinants of both lipid and VA modulation of K2P channel gating.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the Discussion section based on the findings.

claim: The results support the presence of a defined modulatory site within the TREK1 channel structure.
source: While our results support the presence of a defined modulatory site within the TREK1 channel structure, these findings do not preclude a contribution from indirect effects of VAs on membrane lipid composition, as has been recently proposed (Pavel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section based on the overall findings.

claim: The findings do not preclude a contribution from indirect effects of VAs on membrane lipid composition.
source: While our results support the presence of a defined modulatory site within the TREK1 channel structure, these findings do not preclude a contribution from indirect effects of VAs on membrane lipid composition, as has been recently proposed (Pavel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to acknowledge alternative mechanisms.

claim: The location of the TREK1 VA-binding site at a region key to the mechanism by which C-terminal-domain-dependent signals are translated to TM4 would allow both an indirect and direct modulatory effect on channel behavior to feed into a shared common pathway.
source: In this context, the location of the TREK1 VA-binding site described in our study at a region key to the mechanism by which C-terminal-domain-dependent signals (including lipid modulation) are translated to TM4 (Zhuo et al., 2016) and ultimately to the selectivity filter gate would allow both an indirect and direct modulatory effect on channel behavior to feed into a shared common pathway.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis stated in the Discussion section with a citation.
